standard.title: Designed solutions for needs
standard.description: identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced by people to meet personal or local community needs and sustainability
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people (AC9TDEFK01). They can identify design decisions and connect them to a purpose. They have not yet connected design to community-level needs or to sustainability considerations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify how familiar products, services and environments are designed and produced to meet personal or local community needs, including sustainability.

nodes.label: Identifying community needs that design addresses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a personal or local community need and explain how a familiar product, service or environment is designed to meet it
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one community need (e.g. medical care, shelter, healthy food access) and explain how a product, service or environment is designed to meet it
nodes.typical_width: Identify community needs across multiple contexts (health, shelter, food, communication, community access); explain how specific design and production decisions address each need; compare how the same need is met in different ways
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians have long understood their dependence on living systems — for example how the Ngarrindjeri Peoples sustainably make woven items from a grass-like sedge; identify the community need being met and how the design reflects that need
Ask questions about the design of shelters in public spaces (school, sportsground) — identify the community need and how the shelter design addresses it including accessibility

response_modes.reason: Students readily identify that products exist for a purpose but often describe use rather than need — 'it's for sleeping' rather than 'it meets the community's need for shelter'. Multiple community contexts (medical care, shelter, food production, communication) where the need is explicitly named before the design is examined builds the need-first reasoning habit.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations living systems direction is genuinely rich — it connects community need and sustainability to long-standing, place-based design knowledge that predates industrial production, making both dimensions of the descriptor concrete and culturally significant.
success_criteria: Names a specific community need (not just a use)
Explains how a product, service or environment is designed to meet that need

nodes.label: Understanding sustainability in design
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify sustainability considerations in how products are designed and produced
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of sustainability in a design or production context — for example using recycled materials, minimising waste, or protecting a living system
nodes.typical_width: Identify sustainability considerations across multiple design contexts; explain why sustainability matters in design and production; give examples of design decisions that minimise negative environmental impact
wider: Explore how people come up with new ideas or modify existing designs to prevent water wastage — identify the sustainability problem, the design response and why it matters

Explore how local products are designed with waste minimisation in mind — for example using recycled clothing or components when making a costume for a community event; explain the sustainability benefit

response_modes.reason: Sustainability is an abstract concept at Y1-2 level. Students need multiple concrete examples where a specific environmental impact is visible before they can generalise the idea. Water wastage, recycled materials and protected living systems are distinct entry points — each makes a different aspect of sustainability tangible.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one sustainability consideration in a design context
Explains why that consideration matters — what environmental impact it addresses
